lesson.intro: Before anyone sees your code, they see a one-page resume and maybe a GitHub profile, usually for less than a minute. This lesson separates ATS myths from facts, gives you a complete one-page resume for a student with no experience yet, shows real bullet rewrites from weak to strong, and covers projects, GitHub, LinkedIn and how to present the projects you build in Recurse.
objectives: Structure a one-page student resume that passes both the parser and the human skimmer
Separate ATS myths from facts and tailor a resume to a posting in five minutes
Rewrite duty-style bullets as impact bullets with a verb, what, how and a number
Present projects, a GitHub profile and LinkedIn that tell one consistent story
Turn a finished Recurse project into a specific, defensible resume bullet

sections.title: What a resume is for, and who reads it
sections.body:
A popular internship can draw thousands of applications. Yours gets a quick first pass, often well under a minute, from someone deciding one thing: should this person get an interview? A resume is not your life story. It is an argument, on one page, that you can do the job.

Two readers matter:

- **The applicant tracking system (ATS).** Most medium and large companies collect applications in an ATS such as Greenhouse, Lever or Workday. It parses your resume into fields and lets recruiters search, filter and move candidates through stages. The next section separates what it really does from the myths.
- **The human skimmer.** A recruiter, and later an engineer, scans from the top: name and links, school and graduation date, the most recent experience, project names and the tech behind them, skills. They are looking for evidence that you have built real things and can learn fast.

For a student or career changer the rules are simple: **one page**, the strongest evidence near the top, and every line earning its place. Every line is also a promise: an interviewer can point at any bullet and say "tell me more about that", so write only what you can talk about for five minutes.

You will tailor it a little for different roles (backend, frontend, data), but the core stays the same. Keep one master document with everything you have done, and cut a one-page version from it for each kind of role.
sections.code:
What a reviewer reads first, top to bottom
1. Name and links    GitHub? LinkedIn? A portfolio?
2. Education         school, degree, graduation date
3. Top of Experience most recent role, first bullet
4. Project names     what was built, with what tech
5. Skills            does it match the posting?
sections.tip: Read the posting, then make sure your resume uses the same names for the skills you really have. A parser and a skimming recruiter both look for exact terms.
sections.pitfall: Writing for yourself instead of the skimmer. Your favorite detail buried in the fourth bullet of the third project will not be read; put the strongest evidence where the eye lands first.

check.question: An interviewer points at a bullet on your resume and says, "Tell me more about that." What does this tell you about writing bullets?
choices: Only write bullets you can explain in depth, because any line can become a five-minute conversation
Bullets should be vague so they are harder to question
Interviewers only ask about the first bullet
Bullets should list every tool you have heard of
check.explanation: Every line on a resume is fair game in an interview. Vague or inflated bullets fall apart under "tell me more", while a specific bullet you understand becomes an easy, confident story.

sections.title: ATS myths and facts
sections.body:
Few topics attract more bad advice than applicant tracking systems. Here is what is true in general (each company configures its own system, so details vary).

- **Myth: "A robot rejects most resumes before a human sees them."** Fact: an ATS is mainly a database and workflow tool. It stores applications, parses resumes into fields, and lets recruiters search, filter and move candidates through stages. The automatic rejections that do happen usually come from **knockout questions** on the application form, such as work authorization, graduation date or willingness to relocate. Answer those carefully and honestly. Some systems also rank applicants, but the decision to interview is usually made by a person.
- **Myth: "You need a special ATS-friendly template."** Fact: any simple, single-column document with real text and standard headings (Education, Experience, Projects, Skills) parses well. Test yours: open the PDF, select all, copy and paste into a plain text editor. If the text comes out complete and in the right order, a parser can read it.
- **Myth: "Stuff in keywords, or hide them in white text."** Fact: white text is still text once parsed, and a recruiter who reads your parsed profile sees the trick. Use the posting's exact names for skills you really have ("PostgreSQL", not only "Postgres"), in your Skills line and in the bullet where you used them.
- **Myth: "A designed resume stands out."** Fact: tables, text boxes, multiple columns, icons and skill bars are the usual causes of scrambled parsing. Contact details placed in the document's header or footer area are sometimes missed, so put them in the body.
- **Myth: "Never send a PDF."** Fact: modern systems handle text-based PDFs well, and a PDF keeps your layout. Send a PDF unless the posting asks for another format. A scanned PDF is an image and contains no text at all.
- **Myth: "One resume fits every application."** Fact: keep a master version and spend five minutes tailoring each copy: reorder Skills to match the posting, swap in your most relevant project, and use their terms.
- **Myth: "Apply to every role at the company."** Fact: recruiters can see all of your applications. Apply to the one or two roles that fit.

The activity runs a tiny version of what a recruiter's search does: it looks for skills named in a posting and tells you which ones your resume never mentions. Only add the ones you can really discuss.
sections.tip: Name your file clearly, such as Jordan-Lee-Resume.pdf. "resume_final_v3.pdf" is what every reviewer already has twenty of.
sections.pitfall: Answering a knockout question carelessly, such as picking the wrong graduation year or saying you need sponsorship when you do not. Those answers can filter you out automatically, before anyone reads the resume.

activity.title: Check a resume against a posting
activity.prompt: Run it and read which posting skills the resume never mentions. Fix the one that is just a naming mismatch (Postgres versus PostgreSQL) and run it again. Then paste in your own resume text (select all in your PDF, copy, paste) and a real posting.

props.code:
import re

resume = """
JORDAN LEE
jordan@example.com | github.com/jordan-example
EDUCATION
State University, B.S. Computer Science, Expected May 2028
PROJECTS
StudyMatch | Python, Flask, Postgres, React
- Built a study-group matching app used by 300+ students
SKILLS
Python, JavaScript, SQL, Git
"""

posting = """
Software Engineering Intern. Build backend services in Python
and Java, write SQL against PostgreSQL, use Git and Docker,
and write unit tests.
"""

SKILLS = ["Python", "Java", "JavaScript", "TypeScript", "SQL",
          "PostgreSQL", "React", "Flask", "Django", "Docker",
          "Git", "AWS", "Linux", "C++"]
HEADINGS = ["EDUCATION", "EXPERIENCE", "PROJECTS", "SKILLS"]

def has(text, word):
    w = re.escape(word.lower())
    pattern = r"(?<![\w+#])" + w + r"(?![\w+#])"
    return re.search(pattern, text.lower()) is not None

found = [h for h in HEADINGS if h in resume.upper()]
print("Headings:", ", ".join(found))
print("Email found:", bool(re.search(r"\S+@\S+\.\w+", resume)))
wanted = [s for s in SKILLS if has(posting, s)]
missing = [s for s in wanted if not has(resume, s)]
print("Posting asks for:", ", ".join(wanted))
print("Not on the resume:", ", ".join(missing) or "none")
props.task: Change "Postgres" to "PostgreSQL" in the resume and run it again. Add Java or Docker only if you have really used them.

check.question: Which statement about applicant tracking systems is most accurate?
choices: An ATS reads every resume and rejects most of them using artificial intelligence
An ATS can only read Word documents, never PDFs
An ATS mainly stores and parses applications for recruiters to search; automatic rejections usually come from knockout questions on the form
Hiding keywords in white text is the best way to pass an ATS
check.explanation: In general an ATS is a database and workflow tool, and people decide who gets interviews, often after searching or filtering. Knockout questions are the common automatic filter. Text-based PDFs parse well, and white-text keywords show up in the parsed profile and look dishonest.

sections.title: A one-page resume with no experience yet
sections.body:
Here is the skeleton most students should use. The order is the argument: put your strongest evidence where the skimmer looks first.

- **Header.** Name, email, phone, city (optional) and links to GitHub, LinkedIn and a portfolio if you have one. For US applications, no photo, no full street address and no date of birth.
- **Education.** First while you are a student. School, degree, major, expected graduation month and year. GPA if it helps you (a common rule of thumb is 3.0 or higher). Optionally one line of relevant coursework.
- **Projects.** Two to four projects, each with a name, tech stack, link and two or three impact bullets. With no tech experience yet, this goes above Experience, because it is your strongest evidence.
- **Experience.** Reverse chronological: internships, research, TA roles, part-time jobs. A non-tech job belongs here with one or two bullets that show responsibility, reliability or training others.
- **Leadership and activities.** Club roles, hackathons (even ones you didn't win), workshops you ran, tutoring.
- **Skills.** Grouped: Languages, Frameworks and tools. List only what you could answer interview questions about.

Leave out an objective statement ("Seeking a challenging position..."), "References available upon request", lists of soft skills ("team player, hard worker"), unrelated hobbies, and high school details once you are well into college, unless they are remarkable.

Formatting basics that keep a page readable: one font at 10 to 11 points, margins of about half an inch to an inch, bold only for headings and names, dates aligned the same way everywhere, and a consistent date format. Export to PDF.

What if the page looks empty? Do not pad it. Fill it with evidence: finish one or two real projects (the Recurse project briefs are designed for exactly this), add coursework projects that went beyond the assignment, and include any job, club role or hackathon. A half-full page of real work beats a full page of filler, and in a month or two of steady building the page fills itself.

check.question: A second-year student has no internships, two solid deployed projects and a part-time cafe job. Which order makes the strongest case?
choices: Experience (cafe), Education, Projects, Skills
Objective, Skills, Experience, Projects, Education

check.explanation: Education leads while you are a student. The projects are the strongest evidence of software skill, so they go above the cafe job, which still earns a short entry. Objectives and references waste space.

sections.title: Impact bullets: verb, what, how, result
sections.body:
Most student bullets describe duties: "Responsible for the backend." "Worked on a website." They tell a reviewer what you were near, not what you did or how well. A strong bullet follows a formula:

**Action verb + what you built or changed + how (tech or method) + measurable result.**

Laszlo Bock, Google's former head of people operations, popularized a similar version: "Accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z." Either way, each bullet answers three questions: what did you do, with what, and what changed because of it?

- **Start with a strong past-tense verb:** built, designed, implemented, automated, reduced, migrated, optimized, debugged, led, shipped. Use present tense only for a role you still hold.
- **Avoid weak openers:** "helped with", "worked on", "responsible for", "participated in". If you only helped, say what your piece was.
- **Name the tech** where it fits naturally, so the skimmer and the ATS both see it in context.
- **End with a result:** a number (time, users, speed, errors) or concrete evidence (adopted by, still used by, merged into).
- **Keep each to one or two lines,** with two to four bullets per role or project, strongest first.

"But I'm a student, I don't have numbers." You have more than you think. Count users or people who tried it (even 12 classmates), tests and coverage, the size of the data (rows, files, gigabytes), time before and after a change, requests per second in a load test, features shipped, people at a workshop you ran, a hackathon placing. Time a slow operation before you optimize it so you have a "before". When there is truly no number, use scale or adoption: "now used by the club for all event sign-ups".

The code block shows six real rewrites, weak to strong. The activity runs a tiny bullet checker that flags weak openers and bullets with no number. It cannot judge whether a bullet is true or impressive, but it catches the most common problems in seconds.

activity.title: Run the bullet checker
activity.prompt: Run it and read why two bullets get FIX. Rewrite those two using the formula (verb, what, how, result) until every line says OK, then paste in three bullets from your own resume and fix whatever it flags.

props.code:
WEAK_OPENERS = ("helped", "worked on", "responsible for",
                "participated in", "assisted")
STRONG_VERBS = ("built", "designed", "implemented", "automated",
                "reduced", "cut", "migrated", "optimized", "wrote",
                "shipped", "led", "created", "debugged")

bullets = [
    "Worked on the backend for a club app.",
    "Built a Flask REST API for a club events app, "
    "serving 400+ members.",
    "Responsible for testing.",
    # Paste your own bullets here, then run again
]

for b in bullets:
    text = b.lower()
    problems = []
    if text.startswith(WEAK_OPENERS):
        problems.append("weak opener: say what you built")
    elif not text.startswith(STRONG_VERBS):
        problems.append("first word: is it a strong verb?")
    if not any(ch.isdigit() for ch in b):
        problems.append("no number: can you measure the result?")
    if len(b) > 160:
        problems.append("long: aim for one or two lines")
    print("FIX" if problems else "OK ", b)
    for p in problems:
        print("     -", p)
props.task: Rewrite the weak bullets until every line starts with OK.

sections.tip: Keep a running "brag document" during every project and job: what you did, numbers, links. Bullets are easy to write from notes and hard to write from memory.
sections.pitfall: Listing duties instead of results. "Responsible for the database" says nothing about whether the database was any good.

check.question: Which bullet best follows the verb + what + how + result formula?
choices: Reduced API response time from 900 ms to 150 ms by adding Redis caching to the busiest endpoints.
Responsible for the database layer of a group project.
Helped teammates with various coding tasks.
Worked on improving performance using best practices.
check.explanation: It opens with a strong verb, says what changed (API response time), how (Redis caching on the busiest endpoints) and the result (900 ms to 150 ms). The others are duties or vague claims with no evidence.

sections.title: Projects as proof of skill
sections.body:
Without internship experience, projects are your evidence. But not all projects count the same. Reviewers have seen hundreds of to-do apps and weather apps copied from tutorials. What makes a project stand out:

- **It solves a real problem,** ideally for real people: your club, your dorm, a family business, yourself. "Used by 40 people" beats "a clone of Twitter."
- **It goes past the tutorial.** If you started from one, add what it didn't cover: authentication, tests, a deployment, a feature you designed.
- **It is finished and runnable,** with a live demo link or a short GIF, plus clear setup steps.
- **It shows engineering habits:** tests, a sensible structure, meaningful commits, error handling and a README that explains decisions.
- **You can talk about it for 10 minutes:** why you chose that database, what broke, what you would change. Interviewers ask, and depth matters more than the number of projects.

Two or three strong projects beat eight shallow ones. A good set covers different skills: for example, one backend project with an API, a database and tests; one full-stack or frontend project that is deployed; and one that shows algorithms, data or tooling.

On the resume, each project gets a header line (name, tech stack, link) and two or three impact bullets written with the same formula as work experience. The project briefs in Recurse are designed to build exactly this kind of set, and the last section of this lesson shows how to present them.

check.question: Which project is likely to impress a reviewer most?
choices: A to-do app copied step by step from a popular tutorial
A deployed tool your club uses every week, with tests, a README and a clear commit history
Eight small unfinished repositories with no READMEs
A list of every programming language you have tried
check.explanation: Real users, a deployment, tests and documentation show you can finish and maintain software. A copied tutorial shows you can follow steps, and a pile of unfinished repos suggests the opposite of finishing.

sections.title: GitHub: what a reviewer sees in 30 seconds
sections.body:
A reviewer clicks your GitHub link. In about 30 seconds they will see your profile, glance at your pinned repositories, open one and read the top of its README. Make those 30 seconds count.

- **Pinned repositories.** You can pin up to six. Pin your best projects, not forks you never changed or class exercises.
- **Profile README.** A public repository with the same name as your username shows its README on your profile. Use it for a short intro: who you are, what you're building, how to reach you.
- **Each pinned project's README.** The most important part. At the top: one sentence on what it is, a screenshot or GIF, and a demo link. Then how to run it, the tech stack, key features, design decisions and what you learned.
- **Commit history.** Many small commits with clear messages ("Add rate limiting to login endpoint") look like real engineering. One giant "initial commit" looks like an upload.
- **Signs of quality.** Tests, a passing CI badge, a license, a .gitignore, and no build output or node_modules folder committed.
- **No secrets.** Never commit API keys or passwords. Use environment variables and keep .env in .gitignore. If a key ever gets pushed, revoke it right away: deleting the file in a later commit leaves it in the history.

The contribution graph (the green squares) matters much less than people think. A reviewer would rather see one well-documented project than a year of trivial daily commits.
sections.code:
# StudyMatch

Match students into study groups by course and schedule.
Live demo: https://studymatch-demo.example.com

![Demo](docs/demo.gif)

## Features
- Add your courses and free time, get matched into
  groups of 3 to 5
- Email reminders before each session

## Tech stack
Python, Flask, PostgreSQL, React, Docker

## Run it locally
    git clone https://github.com/jordan-example/studymatch
    cd studymatch && cp .env.example .env
    docker compose up

## Design decisions
- Matching runs as a nightly batch job, not on every
  signup: simpler, and fast enough at this scale

## Tests
    pytest    (60 tests, run in CI on every push)

## What I'd do next
- Let groups reschedule sessions without starting over
sections.tip: Ask a friend to open your GitHub cold and tell you after 30 seconds what you build and how good it looks. Fix whatever they missed.
sections.pitfall: Committing a .env file or an API key. Automated scanners find leaked keys in public repositories quickly, and reviewers treat it as a red flag.

check.question: A reviewer opens one of your pinned repositories. What should they see first?
choices: The source tree with no README
A license file and nothing else
A one-sentence description, a screenshot or GIF, and a demo link at the top of the README
A long history of how the project developed
check.explanation: The top of the README is the first thing on the repository page. In a few seconds it should say what the project is, show it working and offer a way to try it. The history and the license matter, but nobody reads them first.

sections.title: Portfolio site and LinkedIn basics
sections.body:
A **portfolio site** is optional for most backend or general software roles, and very useful for frontend roles, where the site itself is a work sample. If you build one, keep it simple:

- One page is enough: a short intro, about three projects (each with a screenshot, a sentence on what it does and links to the demo and the code), your resume as a PDF, and contact links.
- Fast, readable on a phone, no broken links. A free static host such as GitHub Pages or Netlify is plenty.
- A custom domain is a nice touch, not a requirement.

**LinkedIn** is where recruiters search for candidates and where people you ask for referrals will look you up. The basics take about an hour:

- **Photo and headline.** A clear, friendly photo, and a headline that says what you do and want, not just "Student at State University".
- **About.** Three or four sentences: what you build, what you are learning, what you are looking for.
- **Experience and education** that match your resume, with no contradictions in dates or titles.
- **Featured** links to your best project or portfolio.
- **Open to Work.** You can signal that you are looking, either publicly or only to recruiters.
- **A custom profile URL** (linkedin.com/in/your-name) to put on your resume.

Keep the three in sync. Your resume, GitHub and LinkedIn should tell the same story, with the same projects, dates and titles.

sections.tip: Feature the same two or three projects on your resume, your pinned repositories and your portfolio. Consistency makes your story easy to remember.
sections.pitfall: Spending weeks on a portfolio site's animations instead of finishing a project. The projects are the evidence; the site is only the frame.

check.question: Which LinkedIn headline helps a recruiter searching for intern candidates most?
choices: CS student at State | Python, React, PostgreSQL | Seeking Summer 2027 SWE internship
Student
Aspiring developer and lifelong learner
Looking for opportunities
check.explanation: It contains the words recruiters search for (skills, "internship", the season) and says exactly what you want. The others are vague and would not show up in a skills search.

sections.title: Presenting your Recurse projects
sections.body:
Each project brief in Recurse ends with an example resume bullet, showcase ideas and interview talking points. Treat the example bullet as a template, not a line to copy. A reviewer who has seen the same bullet on ten resumes discounts all ten.

Which projects to feature depends on the role. For a backend or general internship, lead with the REST API with a database or the full-stack app, and add the command-line tool or the data structures library as a second project. For a frontend role, lead with the deployed full-stack app or the algorithm visualizer. A merged open-source pull request is strong for any role, because it proves you can work in someone else's codebase.

How to present them:

- **List them under Projects as your own work,** with a name you chose, the tech stack and a link. You built them; there is no need to name the app you learned with. If an interviewer asks where the idea came from, say plainly that you built it from a project spec and then describe what you added.
- **Finish the milestones** to the point where the project runs end to end and has tests. An unfinished project is hard to write a result for.
- **Measure something real.** Count tests and coverage, time a slow operation before and after you optimized it, count users, note the size of the data. Record the numbers in the README as you go.
- **Write the bullet with the formula,** using your numbers and your design decisions. If you built a stretch feature, lead with it: that is the part nobody else has.
- **Make the repository back up every claim.** Pin it, follow the brief's showcase ideas (a GIF and live link at the top of the README, a design notes section) and mention it in your GitHub profile README and LinkedIn Featured section.
- **Prepare the story:** one decision and its trade-off, one bug you fixed, one thing you would change. The talking points in each brief are a starting list.

Never claim what you didn't do. If you followed a guide for part of the project, that is fine; say what you built beyond it. Interviewers dig into the projects on your resume, and the safest bullet is one you can defend line by line.
sections.code:
The brief's example (a template)
- Built a Python command-line task manager with due dates,
  tags and search; wrote 30+ pytest tests.

Your version (your numbers, your stretch feature)
- Built a Python CLI task manager with due-date reminders
  and tag search; wrote 42 pytest tests (95% coverage) and
  packaged it for pip; 6 classmates use it daily.

From the URL shortener brief, after your own load test
- Designed a URL shortener (FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis);
  a cache-aside Redis layer cut p95 redirect latency from
  45 ms to 8 ms at 1,000 requests per second.
sections.tip: Add a "Results" section to each project README with the numbers you measured. It keeps your resume honest and gives interviewers something to read.
sections.pitfall: Pasting the brief's example bullet as-is. It describes the minimum version of the project; your bullet should describe yours.

check.question: You finished the URL shortener brief and load-tested it yourself. Which bullet is best for your resume?
choices: The brief's example bullet, copied exactly
"Followed a project brief to make a URL shortener."
"Expert in distributed systems and scalability."
"Designed a URL shortener (FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis); a Redis cache cut p95 redirect latency from 45 ms to 8 ms in my 1,000 requests-per-second load test."
check.explanation: It names the tech, says what you designed and gives a measured result you can explain. A copied bullet looks identical to other applicants', "followed a brief" undersells the work, and "expert" is a claim an interviewer will test immediately.

keyTerms.definition: Software that stores and parses applications so recruiters can search and filter them.
A resume line with an action verb, what you did, how you did it and a measurable result.
Listing the most recent experience first.
The languages, frameworks and tools a project uses, listed on its header line.
The front page of a repository: what it is, how to run it and why it is built that way.
One of up to six repositories featured at the top of a GitHub profile.
The README of a public repository named after your username, shown on your GitHub profile.
A running log of what you did, with numbers and links, kept so bullets are easy to write later.
The line under your name on LinkedIn; it should name your skills and the role you want.
An application form question, such as graduation date or work authorization, whose answer can filter you out automatically.
A longer private document with everything you have done, from which you cut tailored one-page versions.

summary: A resume is a one-page argument for an interview: single column, standard headings, strongest evidence at the top.
An ATS mostly stores and parses applications for recruiters to search; answer knockout questions carefully and test your PDF by copying its text.
Students lead with Education; put Projects above Experience until you have relevant tech experience.
Write bullets as action verb + what + how + measurable result, and find honest numbers in tests, data size and timings.
Two to four finished projects with tests, demos and clear READMEs beat many shallow repos; pin them and never commit secrets.
Present Recurse projects as your own work with your own numbers and stretch features, and be plain about where the idea came from.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a classmate how to turn "Worked on the backend for a club app" into a strong resume bullet, and what a reviewer should find when they click through to the project on GitHub.

questions.question: How many pages should a student's internship resume be? Answer with a number.
questions.explanation: One page is the norm for students and early-career engineers. Reviewers skim quickly, and a second page usually means weaker material diluting the strong lines.

questions.question: Put the parts of an impact bullet in order.
items: Result: a number or concrete evidence
questions.explanation: Verb, what, how, result. For example: "Cut (verb) page load time (what) by lazy-loading images (how) from 3.8 s to 1.1 s (result)." The order can flex a little, but all four parts should be there.

questions.question: Which item should you leave off a resume for US tech internships?
choices: Your GitHub link
A photo of yourself
Your expected graduation date
The tech stack for each project
questions.explanation: Photos are not expected on US resumes and take space from evidence. Graduation date tells recruiters which internships you qualify for, and links and tech stacks are exactly what technical reviewers look for.

questions.question: Which belong on a student's technical resume? Choose all that apply.
choices: Expected graduation month and year
Links to GitHub and LinkedIn
A part-time job outside tech, with one or two bullets
"References available upon request"
An objective statement
Skill rating bars
questions.explanation: Graduation date, links and any real job all give reviewers useful evidence. "References available" is assumed, objectives say nothing specific, and rating bars are unmeasurable.

questions.question: What is the main problem with this resume bullet?
questions.code: - Responsible for the backend of the club website.
choices: It is too long for one line
It is written in the past tense
It mentions a website
It names a duty instead of what you did, how, and what changed
questions.explanation: "Responsible for" describes a job description, not an achievement. Rewrite with a verb, the work, the tech and a result: "Built the Flask backend and PostgreSQL schema for the club website, serving 400+ members."

questions.question: Match each weak bullet to its stronger rewrite.

pairs.right: Wrote 40 pytest tests that caught 3 regressions before release
Cut page load from 3.8 s to 1.1 s by lazy-loading images
Automated deploys with GitHub Actions, cutting release time from 1 hour to 5 minutes
Shipped a Discord bot that posts deadlines, used by 3 course servers

questions.explanation: Each rewrite swaps a vague opener for a strong verb, says exactly what was done and with what, and ends with a number a reviewer can remember.

questions.question: Choose the opener that makes this the strongest bullet.
questions.code: _____ a REST API in Flask with token authentication, serving 400+ club members.
choices: Built
Helped with
Was responsible for
Participated in
questions.explanation: "Built" says you did the work. "Helped with" and "participated in" hide your contribution, and "was responsible for" describes a duty rather than an achievement.

questions.question: You still work at the campus help desk. Which tense should that role's bullets use?
choices: Past tense, like every other bullet
Future tense, to show ambition
Present tense, since you still hold the role ("Resolve 25+ tickets a week")
Mix tenses freely; nobody notices
questions.explanation: Current roles use present tense and past roles use past tense. Mixing tenses within a role looks careless, and careful reviewers do notice.

questions.question: Which bullet will hold up best when an interviewer asks follow-up questions?
choices: "Improved system efficiency by 47.3% through optimization."
"Leveraged cutting-edge technologies to drive synergies."
"Reduced the nightly import from 40 to 6 minutes by batching database inserts (measured over a week of runs)."
"Expert in Python, Java, C++, Go, Rust and Haskell."
questions.explanation: It names a specific change, a specific method and how it was measured, so every follow-up has an answer. A precise percentage with no method invites doubt, buzzwords say nothing, and claiming expertise in six languages invites a hard quiz.

questions.question: What does an applicant tracking system (ATS) do with your resume?
choices: Parses it into fields and lets recruiters search and filter applications
Automatically rejects any resume without a photo
Runs and grades your code samples
Prints it for the hiring manager
questions.explanation: An ATS stores and parses applications so recruiters can search by skills, school or graduation date. That is why clean formatting and the posting's exact skill names help.

questions.question: In a first pass of well under a minute, what does a reviewer typically look at?
choices: The hobbies section
The font and color scheme
The references
School and graduation date, the most recent experience, and project names with their tech
questions.explanation: Skimmers go top-down looking for eligibility (school, graduation date) and evidence (recent experience, what you built and with what). Put your strongest material where that scan lands.

questions.question: You built a to-do app by following a tutorial. How do you make it resume-worthy?
choices: List it as-is, since every project counts
Add something the tutorial didn't cover (auth, tests, a deployment or your own feature) and explain those decisions in the README
Rename it so it looks original
Delete the README so reviewers can't tell where it came from
questions.explanation: Reviewers recognize tutorial projects. Extending one with real engineering work and documenting your decisions turns it into evidence of your own skill. Hiding where it came from is dishonest and easy to discover.

questions.question: Which make a portfolio project convincing to a reviewer? Choose all that apply.
choices: A live demo or a short GIF
Tests and a README that explains decisions
Real users, even a handful
Being one of many unfinished repositories
A name that sounds impressive
questions.explanation: A demo shows it works, tests and a README show engineering habits, and users show it solves a real problem. Unfinished repos and clever names add nothing.

questions.question: How many projects should a student usually feature on a resume?
choices: Two to four strong ones that show different skills
One, described in full detail
Every project ever started
None, because projects don't count
questions.explanation: Two to four projects fit on one page with real bullets, and covering different skills (backend, deployed full-stack, algorithms or tooling) gives a reviewer a fuller picture.

questions.question: What should you be ready to say about any project on your resume?
questions.answer: The problem it solves and for whom, one important decision and its trade-off, one bug or obstacle and how you solved it, and what you would change or build next.
questions.explanation: Interviewers often spend 10 minutes on one resume project. Depth and honest reflection matter more than the size of the project.

questions.question: How many repositories can you pin to a GitHub profile? Answer with a number.
questions.explanation: GitHub lets you pin up to six repositories (or gists). Use them for your best projects, since pinned repos are the first thing a visitor sees.

questions.question: Which belong in a strong project README? Choose all that apply.
choices: One sentence on what the project does
A screenshot or GIF and a demo link
How to run it locally
Design decisions and trade-offs
Your real API keys, so others can run it
A list of every commit
questions.explanation: What it is, what it looks like, how to run it and why it is built that way are what reviewers want. Keys belong in environment variables (ship a .env.example with placeholders instead), and git already records the commits.

questions.question: You notice you pushed an API key to a public repository last week. What should you do first?
choices: Delete the file in a new commit, which removes the key
Make the repository private and move on
Revoke or rotate the key immediately, then remove it from the code and history and load it from an environment variable
Do nothing, since nobody reads old commits
questions.explanation: Assume the key is already compromised: automated scanners watch public repositories. Revoking it is the only real fix. A new commit leaves the key in the history, and making the repo private doesn't undo a week of exposure.

questions.question: Which commit history looks most like real engineering?
choices: One commit called "initial commit" containing 15,000 lines
Hundreds of commits all named "update"
Daily commits that only change whitespace
Forty small commits with messages such as "Add rate limiting to login endpoint"
questions.explanation: Small commits with descriptive messages show how the project evolved and that you work the way teams do. A single giant commit looks like an upload, and meaningless commits look like gaming the contribution graph.

questions.question: A reviewer opens this repository. What is the biggest problem?
questions.code:
studymatch/
  .env
  app.py
  node_modules/
  README.md
  requirements.txt
  tests/
choices: There is a tests folder at the top level
.env and node_modules are committed; secrets and installed dependencies belong in .gitignore
The README is in the root
app.py should be called main.py
questions.explanation: .env usually holds secrets, and node_modules is installed dependencies that anyone can recreate from the package file. Both should be listed in .gitignore. A tests folder and a root README are good signs.

questions.question: Who gets the most benefit from a personal portfolio site?
choices: Only senior engineers
Frontend candidates, because the site itself is a work sample
Nobody, because recruiters never click links
Only people without a GitHub account
questions.explanation: For frontend roles the site demonstrates the exact skill being hired for. For other roles it is a nice frame for your projects, but finished projects matter more.

questions.question: Your resume says "Help Desk Assistant, Sep 2025 to present" but LinkedIn says "IT Intern, 2024". Why fix it?
choices: LinkedIn rejects profiles with mismatched dates
It doesn't matter; nobody compares them
Recruiters only read LinkedIn, so the resume can say anything
Contradictions make reviewers doubt everything else, so titles and dates should match everywhere
questions.explanation: Recruiters and interviewers do look at both, and a mismatch in titles or dates reads as carelessness or exaggeration. Keep resume, LinkedIn and GitHub telling the same story.

questions.question: Which LinkedIn basics help an internship search? Choose all that apply.
choices: A clear, friendly photo
A headline naming your skills and the role you want
A custom profile URL to put on your resume
A headline that just says "Student"
Dates that differ from your resume
questions.explanation: A photo, a searchable headline and a clean URL make you easy to find and remember. A bare "Student" headline won't match recruiter searches, and mismatched dates raise doubts.

questions.question: Why shouldn't you paste a project brief's example bullet into your resume unchanged?
choices: It describes the minimum version; identical bullets get discounted, and yours should carry your own numbers and decisions
Resumes may not mention projects from a learning app
Example bullets are always too short
Bullets must avoid naming any technology
questions.explanation: The example is a template. Reviewers who see the same line from many applicants learn nothing about you. Your measured results and your stretch features are what make the bullet yours.

questions.question: Put the steps for turning a finished project into a resume bullet in order.
items: Finish the milestones so it runs end to end with tests
Measure something real and record it in the README
Write the bullet: verb, what, how, result
Link the repository and prepare the story behind it
questions.explanation: You need a working project before you can measure it, and numbers before you can write a strong result. Preparing the story last means you can defend every word of the bullet.

questions.question: You followed a tutorial for the first half of a project, then added authentication, tests and a deployment yourself. How should the bullet read?
choices: Claim you designed the whole thing from scratch
Leave the project off entirely
Lead with what you built beyond the tutorial (auth, tests, deployment) and be ready to say what came from the guide
Write only "Followed a tutorial"
questions.explanation: Your own additions are real evidence, so feature them. Being open about the starting point keeps you safe in follow-up questions. Overclaiming is easy to expose, and leaving it off wastes good work.

questions.question: What is the four-part formula for an impact bullet?
questions.answer: Action verb + what you built or changed + how (the tech or method) + a measurable result.
questions.explanation: It answers what you did, with what, and what changed because of it. Google's "accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z" is the same idea in a different order.

questions.question: A posting asks for "PostgreSQL". Your resume mentions "Postgres" once in a project and nowhere in Skills. What is the best fix?
choices: Paste the whole posting into white text at the bottom of the resume
Remove databases from the resume
Use the posting's term, PostgreSQL, in Skills and in the project where you actually used it
List every database you have heard of
questions.explanation: Recruiters search the ATS with the posting's words, so use the same name for a skill you really have, in context. Hidden white text shows up as plain text once parsed and looks dishonest, and listing tools you don't know invites questions you can't answer.

questions.question: A friend says, "Don't bother tailoring; a robot rejects 75 percent of resumes anyway." What is the most accurate reply?
choices: "An ATS mostly stores and parses applications for recruiters to search. Knockout questions can screen people out, so answer them carefully, and tailor so searches find you."
"Right, so send the same resume everywhere."
"Only resumes with a photo get past the ATS."
"The ATS only reads the first line of each resume."
questions.explanation: In general an ATS stores, parses and organizes applications, and recruiters search and filter them; the automatic screen-outs that exist usually come from knockout questions on the form. Viral percentages like this have no reliable source. Tailoring helps because recruiters search with the posting's terms.

questions.question: What is a quick way to check whether a parser can read your resume PDF?
choices: Print it and check that it looks good
Convert it to an image so it looks the same everywhere
Make the file as small as possible
Select all text in the PDF, paste it into a plain text editor, and check it is complete and in order
questions.explanation: Copying all the text into a plain text editor shows roughly what a parser sees. If text is missing or comes out scrambled (columns interleaved, contact details gone), fix the layout. A pretty print preview says nothing about the text layer.

questions.question: Which resume features commonly cause parsing problems? Choose all that apply.
choices: Tables and text boxes
Two or three columns
Contact details placed in the document header area
Standard headings such as Education and Skills
Plain bullet points in a single column
questions.explanation: Tables, text boxes, multi-column layouts and contact details in the header or footer area are the usual causes of scrambled or missing text. Standard section headings help parsers, which is why they are recommended.

questions.question: An application form asks, "Will you now or in the future require visa sponsorship?" Why does answering accurately matter so much?
choices: It only affects which office you sit in
It is optional and recruiters ignore it
The answer changes your resume's font
Answers to knockout questions can filter you automatically, and a wrong answer can cost you the offer later
questions.explanation: Questions like this are knockout questions: the ATS can filter applications on the answer before anyone reads a resume. Answer truthfully (a wrong answer can cost you the offer later), and if you are unsure what applies to you, ask your school's international student office.

questions.question: Put the five-minute tailoring steps for one application in a sensible order.
items: Read the posting and note the skills it names
Reorder Skills so the matching ones come first
Swap in your most relevant project
Use the posting's exact names for skills you have
Check it is still one page and export a clearly named PDF
questions.explanation: Read the posting first so you know what matters, then adjust the parts that change most between roles (skills order, project choice, matching terms), and finish by checking it is still one page and exporting a clearly named PDF.

questions.question: A first-year student has no projects and no tech job, and applications open in two months. What should they do first?
choices: Fill the page with a long objective and soft skills
Wait until next year to write a resume
Build one or two real projects now, and list coursework projects, any job and activities in the meantime
Use a two-page template so it looks fuller
questions.explanation: Two months is enough to finish one or two real projects, which become the strongest part of the resume. Padding with soft skills or a long objective fills space with nothing a reviewer can use, and waiting a year skips first-year programs that do exist.

questions.question: Unless a posting asks for another format, which file format should you send your resume in?
questions.explanation: A text-based PDF keeps your layout identical on every screen and parses well in modern systems. Use the format the posting requests when it names one.

questions.question: What is the most important thing missing from this Education section?
questions.code:
EDUCATION
State University
B.S. Computer Science
Coursework: Data Structures, Algorithms, Databases
choices: A list of every course ever taken
The expected graduation month and year
A high school diploma
The university's address
questions.explanation: Recruiters filter internships by graduation date, because many programs are for students graduating in a particular window. Without it they may skip the resume. GPA is optional, and coursework is a nice extra.

questions.question: Match each vague bullet to the rewrite that adds the method and a number.

pairs.left: Did data work for a research lab
pairs.right: Automated cleaning of 40 GB of sensor data with pandas, turning a 6-hour weekly task into 10 minutes
Tutored 40 intro Python students a semester and wrote 12 practice problems now used in labs
Ran 5 intro Git workshops for about 120 students as ACM workshop lead
Rebuilt the club site in React; it now handles all event sign-ups

questions.explanation: Each rewrite replaces a vague duty with a verb, the specific work, the method and a number or adoption a reviewer can remember.

questions.question: Your class project has no users and no analytics. Where can you honestly find a number for its bullet?
choices: Count tests and coverage, the size of the data, or time an operation before and after you optimized it
Estimate a user count that sounds realistic
Use the grade you hope to get
Leave numbers out of every bullet
questions.explanation: Things you can count or time yourself are honest numbers: tests, coverage, data size, before-and-after timings. Made-up user counts or invented percentages fall apart at the first follow-up question.

questions.question: An interviewer asks, "Was this project your idea?" about an app you built from a Recurse project brief. What is the best answer?
choices: "Yes, I came up with all of it."
"It started from a project spec. I built it myself, and I added offline sync and the tag search, which I can walk you through."
"I'd rather not say."
"No, so it probably doesn't count."
questions.explanation: Being plain about the starting point and specific about your own work is both honest and persuasive. Claiming the idea invites follow-ups you cannot answer, and downplaying the project throws away real evidence.

questions.question: You are applying for a backend internship and have finished three Recurse projects. Which should lead your Projects section?
choices: The algorithm visualizer, because it looks the most impressive
The command-line task manager, because it was the first one finished
The REST API with a database, auth and tests, because it matches the role
A tutorial to-do app, because it is the simplest to explain
questions.explanation: A REST API with a database, auth and tests is direct evidence for backend work, so it goes first. The visualizer is a strong frontend project, the CLI is a good second project, and a tutorial clone is not your own work.
